after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(4)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

Every n×n matrix A can be written in the form

A=PJP−1,

where J is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of A, and P is an invertible matrix.

Notice that A is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue λ=2, and

J=A=2I=[2002].

after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -2 \\ 4 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-2)(4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(-4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -1 \\ 9 & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ 9 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot (9) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & -1 \\ 9 & 1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ 9 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot (9) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$
